Lecture 10: Covariance and Correlation, Conditional Expectation and Variance

Author

Jamie Haddock

Covariance and Correlation

Covariance

\[\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]\]

Definition: uncorrelated

\(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated if \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\).

Facts
  • \(\text{Cov}(X,X) = \text{Var}(X)\)
  • \(\text{Cov}(X, aY+b) = a\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)\)
  • \(\text{Cov}(X, Y+Z) = \text{Cov}(X,Y) + \text{Cov}(X,Z)\)
  • \(X,Y\) independent \(\implies \text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\) (the converse is false – next slide)

Example: Uncorrelated but Not Independent

\((X,Y)\) uniform over the four points \((1,0), (0,1), (-1,0), (0,-1)\) (each with probability \(\tfrac14\))

\(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = 0 - 0\dot 0 = 0\)

However, \(X\) and \(Y\) are not independent since a nonzero value of \(X\) fixes \(Y = 0\) and vice versa.

Correlation

\[\rho(X,Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{var}(X)\text{var}(Y)}} \in [-1, 1]\]

\(\rho\) rescales covariance to be unit-free: \(\rho\) near \(+1\) means a strong positive linear relationship, near \(-1\) a strong negative one, near \(0\) little to no linear relationship.

Code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
rhos = [-0.9, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, 0.9]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(rhos), figsize=(15, 3.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, r in zip(axes, rhos):
    cov_mat = [[1, r], [r, 1]]
    samples = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], cov_mat, 800)
    ax.scatter(samples[:, 0], samples[:, 1], s=4, alpha=0.4, color="C0")
    ax.set_title(fr"$\rho = {r}$")
    ax.set_xlim(-3.5, 3.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-3.5, 3.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Example: Heads and Tails out of \(n\) Flips

\(X\) = # heads, \(Y\) = # tails out of \(n\) independent flips. Since \(X + Y = n\) and \(E[X] + E[Y] = n\), we have \[X - E[X] = -(Y - E[Y]).\]

Thus, \[\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E\left[(X-E[X])(Y-E[Y])\right] = -E\left[(X-E[X])^2\right] = -\text{var}(X).\]

And, \[\rho(X,Y) = \frac{-\text{var}(X)}{\sqrt{\text{var}(X)^2}} = -1.\]

Fact

\(\rho = 1\) or \(-1\) \(\iff\) \(Y - E[Y] = c\,(X - E[X])\) for some constant \(c\) (a perfect linear relationship). Here \(c=-1\).

Variance of a Sum of RVs

\[\text{Var}\Big(\sum_i X_i\Big) = \sum_i \text{Var}(X_i) + \sum_{i \ne j} \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\]

Proof \[\text{Var}\Big(\sum_i X_i\Big) = E\Big[\Big(\sum_i (X_i - EX_i)\Big)^2\Big] = \sum_i \sum_j E[(X_i-EX_i)(X_j-EX_j)]\] Splitting the double sum into \(i=j\) and \(i \ne j\) terms gives \(\sum_i \text{Var}(X_i) + \sum_{i\ne j}\text{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\). (The second sum is over ordered pairs, so it’s the same as \(2\sum_{i<j}\text{Cov}(X_i,X_j)\).)

If all pairs are uncorrelated (in particular if the \(X_i\) are independent), every covariance term vanishes and this collapses to the familiar \(\text{Var}(\sum_i X_i) = \sum_i \text{Var}(X_i)\).

Example: The Hat-Check Problem, Revisited

Recall the previous example: \(n\) people’s hats are shuffled and returned at random; \(X\) = number of people who get their own hat back, \(X=\sum_i X_i\) where \(X_i\) indicates person \(i\) getting their own hat. We showed \(E[X]=1\) for every \(n\). Now: \(\text{Var}(X)\)?

Because \(X_i\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(p = 1/n\), we have \[\text{Var}(X_i) = \tfrac1n - \tfrac1{n^2} = \tfrac{n-1}{n^2} \text{ and } E[X_i] = 1/n,\]

so \[ \begin{aligned} \text{Cov}(X_i,X_j) &= E[X_iX_j] - \frac{1}{n} \frac{1}{n} = P(X_i =1, X_j =1) - \frac{1}{n^2} \\&= P(X_i = 1)P(X_j = 1 \mid X_i = 1) - \frac{1}{n^2} = \tfrac{1}{n(n-1)} - \tfrac1{n^2} = \tfrac{1}{n^2(n-1)} \;\; (i\ne j) \end{aligned} \]

Thus,

\[\text{Var}(X) = n\cdot\frac{n-1}{n^2} + n(n-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n^2(n-1)} = \frac{n-1}{n} + \frac1n = 1\]

\(\text{Var}(X) = 1\) for every \(n \ge 2\).

Conditional Expectation & Variance

Law of Iterated Expectation

\(E[X\,|\,Y]\) is itself a random variable: its value depends on the outcome of \(Y\). \(E[X\,|\,Y{=}y]\) is an ordinary function of \(y\); plugging in the random \(Y\) makes \(E[X\,|\,Y]\) random too.

Law of Iterated Expectation (LIE)

\[E\big[E[X\,|\,Y]\big] = E[X]\]

Example: Random Coin Bias

A coin’s probability of heads \(Y\) is itself random (\(Y \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\)). Given \(Y=y\), the number of heads \(X\) in \(n\) flips is \(\text{Binomial}(n,y)\). What is \(E[X]\)?

\[E[X\,|\,Y] = nY \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E[X] = E[nY] = n\,E[Y] = \frac n2\]

Example: Averaging Quiz Scores by Section

A class has \(n\) students and the \(i\)th student’s quiz score is \(x_i\), with the class’s average \[m = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i.\] The students are divided into \(k\) disjoint sections \(A_1, \cdots, A_k\) and section \(A_i\) has \(n_i\) students. The average score in section \(i\) is \[m_i = \frac{1}{n_i} \sum_{i \in A_i} x_i.\]

The average over the whole class can be computed as a weighted average of the section averages: \[\sum_{s=1}^k \frac{n_s}{n} m_s = \sum_{s=1}^k \frac{n_s}{n} \frac{1}{n_s} \sum_{i \in A_s} x_i = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{s=1}^k \sum_{i \in A_s} x_i = m.\]

We can see this same calculation through the conditional expectation lens:

Consider an experiment where a student is selected uniformly at random. Consider \(X\) to be the quiz score of the student, and \(Y\) to be the section of the student.

We have \(E[X] = m\) and \(E[X \mid Y = s] = m_s\), then \[m = E[X] = E[E[X\mid Y]] = \sum_{s=1}^k E[X\mid Y=s] P(Y = s) = \sum_{s=1}^k \frac{n_s}{n} m_s.\]

Conditional Expectation as an Estimator

Write \(\hat X = E[X\,|\,Y]\) (the estimator) and \(\tilde X = X - \hat X\) (the estimation error), so \(X = \hat X + \tilde X\).

Facts
  • Estimator is unbiased: \(E[\tilde X] = E[X] - E[\hat X] = E[X]-E[X] = 0\) (by LIE).
  • Uncorrelated with the error: \(\text{Cov}(\hat X, \tilde X) = 0\), since conditioning on \(Y=y\) makes \(\hat X\) a constant and \(E[\tilde X\,|\,Y{=}y]=0\).
  • Consequently \(\text{Var}(X) = \text{Var}(\hat X) + \text{Var}(\tilde X)\).

The picture: \(\hat X(y)\) is the conditional-mean curve; \(\tilde X\) is the scatter of points around it, and that scatter is – on average – unrelated to where you are on the curve.

Code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)

def draw(n):
    Y = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)
    Xhat = Y**2                               # conditional mean E[X|Y=y] = y^2
    X = rng.normal(Xhat, 0.08, n)             # X | Y=y ~ N(y^2, 0.08^2)
    return Y, Xhat, X, X - Xhat

# a modest sample for a readable scatter plot...
Y, Xhat, X, Xtilde = draw(3000)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.3))

yy = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
axes[0].scatter(Y, X, s=4, alpha=0.25, color="C0", label="samples (Y, X)")
axes[0].plot(yy, yy**2, color="C1", lw=2, label=r"$\hat X(y) = E[X|Y=y] = y^2$")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Y")
axes[0].set_ylabel("X")
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].set_title("Conditional mean curve")

axes[1].scatter(Y, Xtilde, s=4, alpha=0.25, color="C2")
axes[1].axhline(0, color="gray", ls="--", lw=1)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Y")
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\tilde X = X - \hat X$")
axes[1].set_title("Residuals: no visible trend with Y")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Conditional Variance

We now define the random variable \[\text{Var}(X\,|\,Y) = E\left[(X - E[X\mid Y])^2 \mid Y\right] = E[\tilde{X}^2 \mid Y].\]

Law of Total Variance

\[\text{Var}(X) = E\big[\text{Var}(X\,|\,Y)\big] + \text{Var}\big(E[X\,|\,Y]\big)\]

Derivation This is exactly the previous slide’s decomposition \(\text{Var}(X)=\text{Var}(\hat X)+\text{Var}(\tilde X)\), rewritten: the “estimator variance” term \(\text{Var}(\hat X) = \text{Var}(E[X|Y])\) is the between-group variance, and the “error variance” term \(\text{Var}(\tilde X) = E[\text{Var}(X|Y)]\) is the within-group variance, since \(E[\tilde X^2\,|\,Y{=}y] = \text{Var}(X\,|\,Y{=}y)\) (the conditional mean of \(\tilde X\) given \(Y=y\) is \(0\)).

Example: Biased-Coin Example, Variance

Continuing the random-bias coin: with \(Y\sim\text{Uniform}(0,1)\), \(X\,|\,Y=y \sim \text{Binomial}(n,y)\), \[ \begin{aligned} E[\text{Var}(X|Y)] &= E[nY(1-Y)] = n(E[Y] - \text{Var}(Y) - (E[Y])^2) = n\Big(\tfrac12-\tfrac{1}{12} - \tfrac{1}{4}\Big) \\&= \frac n6 \end{aligned} \]

Then, \[\text{Var}(E[X|Y]) = \text{Var}(nY) = n^2 \cdot \tfrac1{12}\]

and, \[\text{Var}(X) = \frac n6 + \frac{n^2}{12} = \frac{n(n+2)}{12}.\]
